summary: Specifies the requirements that Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting protocols must meet to support authorization services on the Internet. It is requirements-only and does not define a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a checklist of what a permission-checking system must be able to do, written before anyone builds the system.

questions: what must an authorization protocol support
what must an aaa protocol support
subtitle: A comprehensive requirements checklist for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting protocols.

tldr.problem: AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) protocols must support many different Internet applications with diverse needs. A protocol that works only for one scenario will not serve the Internet broadly.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies detailed requirements for AAA protocols across eleven categories: authorization information representation, security, time handling, network topology support, proxying, trust models, session management, administration, efficiency, system interfaces, and protocol negotiation.
tldr.outcome: The requirements list serves as a specification checklist for designing AAA protocols that are general enough to work across roaming, mobile networks, printing, commerce, and education applications—and secure and flexible enough for future ones not yet imagined.

today: RFC 2906 is an Informational document that serves as a comprehensive requirements specification for AAA authorization protocols. Modern AAA systems, including those used in roaming networks, mobile access, VoIP, and enterprise identity management, are designed with reference to these requirements. The document remains highly relevant as Internet services continue to need flexible, secure, and interoperable authorization mechanisms.

sections.title: From Examples to Requirements
sections.content:
This document is the third in a series on AAA authorization architecture. The first document presented a framework for thinking about authorization; the second showed detailed examples from six applications. This document extracts and formalizes the requirements those applications demonstrated they need.

The requirements are not meant to be orthogonal (some overlap with or repeat others), but rather to capture the full range of what authorization systems must support. The document uses RFC 2119 key words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) to indicate requirement levels. Each requirement is presented as a concise statement followed by explanatory material and sometimes examples.
sections.plainLanguage: This looks at the real examples from before and writes down exactly what a permission system has to be able to do.

sections.title: Core Authorization Requirements
sections.content:
Authorization decisions must be based on information about who is asking, what service they want, and what the operating environment is. This information must be representable as sets of attributes (required) or objects (optional). A single AAA message must carry authorization information for multiple services, and standard attributes should be defined once for use across many applications. Other protocols must define application-specific attributes, and administrators must define custom ones for their environments. Authorization is not limited to identity attributes; role-based access control, clearances, and groups must be supported.

Authorization information must be communicated securely with authenticity, integrity, and privacy mechanisms. Different parts of an authorization package may have different security requirements. The protocol must prevent intermediate administrators from breaching security and must not create replay attack vulnerabilities. Protocols must specify secure defaults that implementations must use unless explicitly configured otherwise.

Authorization information must be timely and expire; no authorization should be valid forever. Mechanisms must support revocation before expiry and time-dependent results. Authorization may be issued long before decisions are made (supporting pre-paid scenarios). The protocol must support both transaction-based (one-shot) and session-based (continuing) authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: An authorization system needs to understand who, what, and where. It must protect information, let things expire, and handle both one-time and ongoing decisions.

sections.title: Network Topology and Trust
sections.content:
AAA protocols must support push, pull, and agent models for authorization delivery. The protocol must work across security and administrative domain boundaries. Roaming must be supported, meaning users from one domain can be served by another. An authorization decision may be made before a requestor has any network connection, so protocols must protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.

The protocol must support intermediate AAA entities (brokers) that participate in authorization without owning end entities or authorization data. These brokers may return forwarding addresses and help parties discover each other. Application-layer proxying must work without introducing security weaknesses. AAA entities must be discoverable, and if requestors provide discovery information, that information must be verifiable in a trusted manner.

AAA entities must make decisions about which other entities they trust for which authorization information. Trust must not be all-or-nothing; an entity might trust another for some purposes but not others. Organizations must be able to configure mutually-trusting local entities with external trust flowing only through designated gateways. An authorization decision might result in "not ready" rather than yes or no, and sessions may be modified without destroying other session information.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks need different ways of asking for authorization. Users should be able to roam. Trust should be specific, not all-or-nothing. Systems should handle failures gracefully.

sections.title: Administration and Efficiency
sections.content:
Authorization data must be administrable on behalf of end entities and AAA entities. Protocols should support centralizable administration, and let users (not just administrators) authorize transactions. One AAA entity may create authorization rules for another (supporting delegation). When an AAA entity fails, the protocol should support recovery—other entities should query its state and re-establish sessions. Hot failover must be possible without losing state.

Authorization and authentication should be separable when needed, but a single message must allow both. AAA protocol data units must be embeddable in other protocols to minimize round trips. State replication should be possible to support resiliency and failover. The protocol should support gateway functions to legacy protocols like RADIUS. It must support a wide range of data types and optimize transport for small packets in a stream between hosts, with flow control for efficient buffer management. Load balancing across multiple servers must be supported.

Negotiation between peers regarding authorization packages must be possible. Peers declare capabilities, and different entities in a chain may support different packages. Negotiation must not be vulnerable to bidding-down attacks that force weak options. Peers must not send unnego attributes, and implementations must reject violations and alert administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should work efficiently without unnecessary round trips. Servers should be able to talk about what they both understand. Things should keep working when servers crash or need updates.

sections.title: A Comprehensive Design Checklist
sections.content:
These requirements span all aspects of an AAA protocol: what information it carries, how it secures that information, how it handles time and sessions, how it routes requests across networks, how it establishes and maintains trust, how it administers data, and how it negotiates capabilities. No single requirement specifies the exact protocol mechanism—rather, they define what must be possible.

A protocol meeting these requirements can support authorization across roaming networks, mobile devices, bandwidth allocation, printing, commerce, education, and applications not yet imagined. The requirements document serves as a design checklist and acceptance test for any AAA protocol claiming to be general-purpose. The work reflected in these requirements continues to influence the design of modern authentication and authorization systems across the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: These requirements are like a checklist: any permission system that wants to work across the whole Internet needs to be able to do all these things.
